name: Jumping / basketball / swimming for height
lead: Jumping drills, basketball and swimming are the sports that height-focused communities most often pair with the goal of a taller adult frame. The reasoning is that repeated impact loading and stretching during the teenage growth years nudges the long bones to grow a little more and keeps the spine long and decompressed, so a person stands taller and carries himself more upright. Even where the extra-height claim is set aside, these sports build the long, lean legs, broad shoulders and upright posture that make a physique look taller and more athletic, and basketball and swimming are also common ways teenagers stay active through puberty.

Reference sources describe adult height as largely heritable, with twin studies putting 60 to 80 percent of height differences down to genes, and with childhood nutrition and health as the main environmental influences.[1] Lengthwise growth takes place at the growth plates (epiphyseal plates), cartilage zones near the ends of long bones where growth hormone drives cartilage cells to multiply before the cartilage is replaced by bone; rising estrogen in puberty, in both sexes, leads the plates to close, typically between about 14 and 17 in boys and 12 to 15 in girls.[2]

Research on exercise and stature is a small, mixed literature. A 1994 analysis of habitually active and inactive boys found no difference in final stature or in the timing and size of the growth spurt,[3] whereas 2025 controlled trials in Chinese children with short stature reported greater height gain after 24 weeks of a jumping program than in non-exercising controls.[4][5] A 2024 mouse study found that cyclic loading of one tibia increased its longitudinal growth.[6] Part of basketball's and swimming's association with height is selection: elite squads are drawn from tall people, and the Wikipedia article on height in sports notes that elite swimmers are generally taller than the population and that drag does not rise with body length.[7][7]

angle.text: Proponents play these sports in adolescence hoping to squeeze out extra growth and keep the spine long. Whatever the effect on stature, regular jumping and swimming also build legs, shoulders and posture that read as a taller, more proportioned silhouette.

paras: Proponents recommend regular jumping exercises, basketball and swimming during puberty, usually alongside sleep and nutrition advice. Jumping and basketball are credited with mechanically stimulating long-bone growth through repeated impact, while swimming is credited with stretching the body and decompressing the spine. Forum members also build routines on Maasai-style jumping, and ask directly whether taking up basketball will make them taller.[9][10][11]

Adumu, also called the Maasai jumping dance, is performed by young Maasai warriors in Kenya and Tanzania at weddings and other ceremonies: dancers stand in a circle and take turns leaping while keeping the body as straight as possible, and are judged on the height of the jump as well as grace. Wikipedia's description makes no health or height claims and suggests the dance may have developed as combat training.[8]

Beyond the growth claim, jumping develops the calves, quadriceps and glutes, swimming develops the lats and shoulders, and both encourage an upright carriage. These changes alter the visual proportions of the body and are a reason practitioners continue even when the height effect is uncertain. Wikipedia notes that taller swimmers also tend to have larger muscles, hands and feet for propulsion.[7]

sections.h: Growth plates, growth and the spine
paras: The growth plate has five zones: a reserve zone, a proliferation zone where growth hormone stimulates cartilage cells to divide, a maturation and hypertrophy zone, a calcification zone, and an ossification zone where bone replaces cartilage.[2] Growth slows and stops as estrogen increases cartilage-cell death and the plate is replaced by bone, after which the plate is visible as an epiphyseal line.[2] Wikipedia's article on human height gives growth in girls as largely ending around 15-16 and in boys continuing to about 18-19, with limited evidence of minor growth after 19, and describes genetic potential, hormones, illness and nutrition as the basic determinants.[1]

Proponents often cite Wolff's law. Julius Wolff, a German anatomist and surgeon, described how healthy bone adapts to the loads placed on it: more loading makes it remodel to become stronger, less loading reduces density; weightlifters show increased bone density and tennis players' racquet-arm bones are stronger than the other arm.[12] The law concerns the density and internal structure of bone rather than its length; one looksmax.org member who posted a self-styled systematic review of jumping and height made that point and argued that no one had yet provided evidence that jumping increases height.[9]

Height also changes over the day. Wikipedia reports that in one study 100 children lost on average 1.54 cm between getting up and late afternoon, that exercise immediately before measuring tends to reduce measured height, and that lying down for a while tends to increase it.[1] A 1990 laboratory study of eight men found that five sets of five drop jumps from one metre shortened stature by about 1.7-1.8 mm, and that gravity inversion afterwards increased stature by 5.18 mm compared with 0.76 mm for standing, with the difference gone by about 30 minutes into recovery.[13] That study measured short-term spinal shrinkage and recovery, not growth.

Elite basketball squads contain many tall players: a 2007-08 NBA survey listed the average player at 6 ft 6 in (1.98 m) in shoes, against about 5 ft 9.3 in for the average American man, and the league switched in 2019-20 to measuring players without shoes, after which many listed heights fell by one to three inches.[7] Swimmers are generally taller than the general population; Wikipedia gives Michael Phelps's height as 1.93 m and the average of eight 100 m freestyle finalists at the US Olympic Trials as 1.95 m, and explains that total drag does not rise with height because wave-making drag falls as body length increases.[7] The same article lists shorter successful swimmers, such as Kosuke Kitajima at 1.77 m.[7]

Studies of athletes mostly examine who is selected and who succeeds. A ten-year prospective study of 85 top-level male water polo players found that swimming capacities and anthropometric indices measured at ages 17-18 predicted later career success in a position-specific way, which concerns selection and performance, not growth caused by the sport.[14] Forum users also relay anecdotes of teenagers who played basketball and grew several inches, with replies attributing this to genetics.[10]

Human trials of jumping and height are recent and small. In 2025 a prospective controlled trial in China followed 47 prepubertal children aged 8-11 with short stature (20 in a jumping group, 27 controls). The jumping group did a progressive program three times a week for 24 weeks; they gained 4.2 cm in height versus 2.48 cm in controls and improved femoral-neck bone mineral density Z-scores, with a mediation analysis suggesting the height effect operated through femoral-neck bone density change, while lumbar-spine density did not differ. The authors suggested high-impact activity might be a useful adjunct for growth and called for further study.[4]

A second 2025 non-randomized controlled study from the same group compared 15 short-stature children doing 24 weeks of jumping with two control groups (20 children with normal growth, 27 with short stature). The exercise group grew more than the short-stature controls and had higher IGF-1 and a higher IGF-1/IGFBP-3 ratio, lower IGFBP-3, and no difference in morning growth hormone.[5] Both are non-randomized studies of children with short stature, not of healthy adolescents seeking extra height, and neither measured adult height.

Earlier work points in several directions. A 1994 review of habitual physical activity and training in boys found that active and inactive boys did not differ in stature, age at peak height velocity or growth rate; swimmers, track athletes and rowers were already taller than reference data in childhood, and gymnasts shorter, which the author read as selection and maturity effects rather than training effects.[3] Also in 1994, a nutrition study in 20 children aged 24-48 months recovering from severe malnutrition found that those encouraged to play and climb grew 22 mm in length over six weeks versus 14 mm in controls, and that malnourished rats forced to be active grew more in length; the setting was recovery from malnutrition, not healthy growth.[15]

In animals, a 2024 study applied cyclic compressive loading to one tibia of juvenile mice for four weeks and reported that loaded bones grew longer than unloaded contralateral bones, with taller growth plates and higher PTHrP expression in female mice.[6] No trial has tested whether swimming or basketball increases final height in healthy adolescents.

Jumping sports carry ordinary sports-injury patterns. A systematic review of ankle injury found the ankle to be the second most commonly injured body site after the knee across 70 sports, with a high incidence in court and team sports including basketball.[16] A meta-analysis of prevention programmes in basketball examined lower-extremity injuries, ankle sprains and ACL tears.[17] Reviews of non-contact ACL injuries in team-ball sports (45 studies; 55 percent of ACL injuries were non-contact) and of adolescent athletes (girls had a higher overall ACL rate than boys, relative risk 1.40) describe jumping, landing and cutting as common mechanisms.[18][19] A 2024 systematic review covers injuries in basketball players generally.[20] A school-based neuromuscular training programme was tested in a randomized trial for lowering sport-related injury incidence.[21]

Adolescents have specific growth-related overuse conditions. Osgood-Schlatter disease, an irritation of the growth plate at the top of the shinbone, is described as caused by repeated tension and is linked to sports with frequent running or jumping; one study cited reports about 9.8 percent of 12-15-year-olds affected, and symptoms usually stop once growth slows.[22] Sever's disease (calcaneal apophysitis), the most common cause of heel pain in children, is linked to basketball and similar sports, and a 2024 review of eight randomized trials reported that conservative treatments such as insoles, exercises and taping were effective for symptoms.[23]

timeline.event: Julius Wolff's work on bone adaptation to load (cited in its 1892 German edition) sets out what became known as Wolff's law.[12]
Laboratory study measures spinal shrinkage after drop jumping and recovery with gravity inversion in eight men.[13]
Reviews report no stature difference between active and inactive boys, and faster length gain in active malnourished children and rats.[3][15]
The NBA moves to measuring player heights without shoes; many listed heights drop by one to three inches.[7]
Ten-year prospective study in male water polo players links body build and swimming tests at 17-18 to later success.[14]
Mouse study reports longer tibiae after cyclic loading; looksmax.org member posts a self-styled review of jumping and height.[6][9]
Two 24-week jumping trials in children with short stature report greater height gain than controls.[4][5]

lore.intro: Height forums commonly list jumping, basketball and swimming among natural measures to maximise growth in the teen years, and Maasai-style jumping appears regularly as a proposed routine; some members also post critical reviews of the claims.[9][10][11]

claims.claim: Basketball and jumping stimulate the growth plates
claims.believers: Proponents say impact loading signals bones to grow, point to tall basketball players, and share stories of teenagers who grew after taking up the sport; members also ask whether taking up basketball will make them taller.[10][11]
claims.experts: Reference sources attribute most height variation to genetics and nutrition; a 1994 analysis found no stature difference between active and inactive boys, and two small 2025 trials in short-stature children reported greater 24-week height gain with jumping.[1][3][4][5]

claims.claim: Swimming decompresses the spine and adds height
claims.believers: Supporters describe swimming as stretching the body in water and lengthening the spine over time.
claims.experts: Laboratory work shows spinal length changes during the day and with loading and inversion that recover within about half an hour; no published study measured lasting height change from swimming in healthy adolescents.[1][13]

claims.claim: Maasai-style jumping explains tall, lean physiques and works as a height routine
claims.believers: Forum guides present adumu-style jumping as a traditional practice and model routines on it.[9]
claims.experts: Adumu is documented as a ceremonial warrior dance judged on jump height and grace, and Wikipedia's description makes no health or height claim; no study links it to stature.[8]

claims.claim: Wolff's law shows that jumping makes bones longer
claims.believers: Proponents cite Wolff's law as the mechanism for impact-driven growth.[9]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes the law as concerning bone density and structure adapting to load; a looksmax.org review-style post makes the same distinction between density and lengthwise growth, and a 2024 mouse study reported growth-plate responses to loading.[12][9][6]

claims.claim: Tall athletes show that these sports make people taller
claims.believers: Members note that many basketball players and swimmers are tall and relay anecdotes of late growth after taking up the sport.[10]
claims.experts: Studies of elite players, such as a ten-year water polo study, examine selection and prediction of success, and the NBA's 2019-20 shift to barefoot measurement lowered many listed heights by one to three inches.[14][7]

claims.claim: Jumping sports are safe for growing teenagers
claims.believers: Supporters present basketball and jumping as ordinary healthy activity for adolescents.
claims.experts: Reviews report common ankle, knee and ACL injuries in jumping and landing sports, and adolescent overuse conditions such as Osgood-Schlatter disease and Sever's disease are linked to jumping and running.[16][18][19][22][23]

card.summary: Sports like basketball and swimming are said to add height, but no trial tests it.
card.note: Tall athletes are common because of selection; no study shows the sports cause extra height.

quick.overview:
Some communities say jumping, basketball and swimming stimulate growth plates or stretch the spine during puberty.

No published trial has tested whether these sports raise final height; athlete studies mostly reflect which tall players are selected.
quick.mechanism: Believers describe mechanical loading of bones and spinal decompression as the mechanisms. Reference sources instead emphasise genetics and nutrition as the main drivers of height.
quick.risks: The sports carry ordinary sports-injury risks. No height-specific harms are documented.
